passages.label: A
passages.text: A short shower can be almost over when a rain gauge records its first tip. What happens inside the gauge before that moment? That number begins with a small opening at a weather station. The opening covers a set area. A wider opening would catch more water from the same rain. To turn the amount of water into a depth, an observer needs to know the size of the opening. That is how a rain gauge can turn precipitation into a reading.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The Met Office says that many rain gauges use a round collector and a funnel. Water goes into the collector and down the funnel. Its narrow end lets water reach the bottle or bucket below. If leaves drop into the top, the narrow end helps keep them out of the measuring mechanism. It also limits how much water can go back into the air on a hot day. A storage gauge holds the rain in a bottle. An observer can pour the rain from the bottle into a glass marked in millimetres.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A tipping-bucket gauge has two small buckets. One fills and tips when there is enough water. Then the other can fill. Even in humid air, the inside may begin dry. People may believe it counts drops and then discover how it really works. A worker checks carefully. People may prefer to take out any leaves first to prevent a blockage, which can cause an unusual result.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Each tip makes the running total increase by a set amount. In that design, five tips show that one millimetre of rain has been recorded. The time of each tip also goes into the record. If the tips come farther apart, the rate may decrease. The total can still go up. A short, hard shower can give the same total as light rain that lasts much longer. A huge storm can spread across several towns, yet each gauge tells us about one place.

passages.label: E
passages.text: People need to be careful when they use one figure from the record. The maximum daily total for a month gives the amount that fell on the wettest day, while the times of the tips show when it rained most heavily on that day. To decide whether two places received the same amount, compare readings taken over the same length of time. Taken together, the readings and the times help a reader tell how much rain there was and how quickly it came down. Nearby observers may hear thunder or see lightning. A short but severe storm may not match the total for a cool day with gentle, long-lasting rain.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The field can still be dry when people hear thunder. The warning matters before rain starts to fall. It is the sound made by lightning and gives an outdoor group a reason to act. The US National Weather Service explains that a strike can reach an area outside the main rain. Looking only for precipitation can leave people in a dangerous place after they have already heard a warning.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The group should stop the activity and go straight to a substantial building with wiring or plumbing. A school building, for example, can offer shelter. Where no suitable building is nearby, an enclosed vehicle with a metal roof and shut windows is another option. A roof may cover the benches beside a field, but a small open shelter is unsafe in a thunderstorm. Someone at the far end of a field may need longer to reach the door than someone beside it. Knowing where everyone should go saves time as soon as the group hears the warning.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A stronger building gives the energy of a strike routes to the ground, although contact with wiring and plumbing can still be dangerous. An organiser can explain carefully why a person might believe a small open cover is enough. Keeping out of the rain is useful as a way to stay dry. But it does not prevent harm when a storm can cause a strike nearby. A vehicle with a closed metal roof may become the more practical choice when no suitable building is close. Taking the warning seriously can save time and reduce the risk of injury.

passages.label: D
passages.text: When the rain stops and the noise starts to drop, a storm can seem almost over even though another flash is still possible. The National Weather Service gives a minimum wait of 30 minutes from the final sound of thunder before people go out again. Even if the rain did not last long, another clap means the group must start the wait again.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Careful planning makes this easier to put into practice. The weather service recommends assigning someone to monitor the weather and call a stop, because a coach or referee may be too busy with the game. A forecast gives the group time to move a game indoors before it starts. The group can decide where to go and share that plan ahead of time. Waiting to agree on the shelter can increase the time people spend outdoors after a warning. A good plan makes clear who speaks and where everyone goes. The first sign may be an unusual sound on a cool afternoon. Some people prefer to assign someone to watch the weather before the event begins.

R_H3.passageTitle: Reading the Heat in Death Valley

passages.label: A
passages.text: In Death Valley National Park, a forecast for the low valley describes only one part of the whole desert. The valley gets very little precipitation, and plants cover only small parts of its dry floor. The US National Park Service explains that clear, dry air and the limited plant life let sunlight heat the ground strongly. A careful comparison of weather reports starts with the place and time they describe. Both can change what a visitor should expect.

passages.label: B
passages.text: On a summer day, the maximum temperature in the low valley can reach 49 degrees Celsius. The minimum reading for the night is just as useful to a visitor. Temperatures usually rise during the day and fall after sunset. On some summer nights, the air in the valley is still around 30 degrees Celsius at its coolest. For visitors who plan to stay out after dark, this can make a real difference. A daily high tells people how hot the air may get. A more detailed forecast shows whether that heat is likely to last into the time when they plan to be outside.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Height changes the comparison. According to the park service, higher ground is generally cooler than the low valley. Temperatures usually decrease by about two to three degrees Celsius for every 300 metres the land rises. Air temperatures may drop on a short drive as the road climbs. Two places that look almost side by side on a map can have different weather also. Each place needs its own forecast.

passages.label: D
passages.text: These comparisons help visitors decide which activities fit the conditions. On hot days, the park advises people to avoid hikes in the low valley and points to higher ground for cooler summer walks. The risks of heat can increase over a long outing, especially when there is little shade. A person who makes a brief stop near a cool building spends little time outside, whereas someone who leaves the same car park for a long walk can spend much longer in dangerous heat.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A visitor might believe every point in the valley has a similar temperature. A closer look helps people discover differences between a dry valley floor and higher ground where an evening can feel cool and sometimes humid. The land can also affect where wildlife rests and where a person might prefer to walk. Check the location carefully because a rise in elevation can cause a change in temperature. An unusual reading on one day gives little evidence about global warming without a longer record. A person may begin a day in the valley and finish it on higher ground. The same coat can feel too warm in one place and just right in another.

questions.prompt: Which conditions does the park service link to strong heating of the ground?
options: Dry air with dense plant cover.
Clear, dry air and little vegetation.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could the daily high of 49 degrees Celsius, on its own, be insufficient for someone spending the evening outside?
options: It reports only the temperature on higher ground.
It reports the length of the dry period instead of a temperature.
It does not tell whether the heat will persist at the planned time.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Two stops look close on a map, but the road climbs between them. Why might the second stop feel cooler?
options: It is higher, and air can be cooler there even after a short drive.
A shorter drive means that the daily high is measured earlier.
The two stops have to share one temperature because they are nearby.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which checks does the author start with when comparing weather reports?
options: Which report gives the larger number and which route is longer.
How clear the air is and which site has less vegetation.
Where each report applies and when it applies.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What distinguishes the two people who start by the same car park?
options: They are described as starting at different elevations.
They can spend quite different amounts of time in dangerous heat.
They must face the same exposure because they start at the same place.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: A route is low, lengthy and mostly exposed. Which change takes account of both risks identified for a hot day?
options: Choose a shorter outing on higher ground.
Use the same long route and change only the starting car park.
Keep the long low-valley walk but plan to find shade at its very end.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why does the writer end with a coat that feels different across the visit?
options: To show that a person must wear the same clothes at every elevation.
To show that the same person can meet different temperatures as the time and place change.
To show that a single temperature reading predicts how the whole trip will feel.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the article say can affect where animals rest?

The length of a visitor’s walk.
The kind of land in the area.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What principle applies both to comparing temperatures at different heights and to considering one unusual reading?
options: Use each observation only for the places and times it can reasonably represent.
Treat a day’s unusual reading as representative once a location is known.
Prefer whichever reading is warmer, even if the two readings are from different settings.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion best represents the whole article?
options: Compare places and times in the reports, then choose the longest walk that fits the lowest temperature shown.
Choose the same hour for both stops and rely on one forecast if the two locations are close to each other.
